intro: If Keyword Planner shows no volume or no forecast, the phrase probably has very little search history on Google. It may also sit in a sensitive category, or your account may not see numbers yet. Read which message you got, because each one has a different fix. This page covers what each blank means, what it costs you, and fixes you can run today without buying another tool.
tldr: A dash or a blank usually means Google has too little data to calculate a number for that phrase.
A Low search volume status means very little to no search history. Bid, Quality Score and ad edits do not clear it.
Sensitive topics such as health and finance can be blocked. Rephrase the angle, but do not try to dodge the policy.
Test close variants, seed from your own URL, check Google itself, and log the decision with a date before you drop a phrase.
Google does not publish the spend level needed for exact numbers. Check account setup and billing first.

blocks.text: You type a phrase into Keyword Planner and the forecast column stays empty. Or a dash sits where a number should be. Or your Google Ads keyword list tags the phrase as Low search volume. Each one looks similar on screen, but each has a different cause. Read which one you got before you try a fix.
Keyword Planner no search volume: what each blank means

Google's help pages point to three different signals. A dash in the impression share column means there isn't enough data to calculate that number. A Low search volume status means very little to no search history on Google. An error asks you to try different keywords or URLs, and Google says that error appears for very low volume or sensitive keywords.

blocks.text: Why Keyword Planner shows no forecast

Keyword Planner does not show a live count of searches. It reports historical search data from Google, plus forecasts that move with recent activity. When that history is thin, there is nothing solid to show. Google's help pages say keywords with very low search volumes, or sensitive keywords, aren't discoverable or forecastable. A blank is often Google declining to guess, not a verdict on your idea.
Average monthly searches and the forecast window

Two numbers show up on most Keyword Planner screens, and they measure different things. Average monthly searches covers a keyword and its close variants, averaged over a 12-month period by default. Forecasts use the last 7 to 10 days, adjusted for seasonality, and refresh daily. A phrase can look healthy in the average and weak in the forecast. Pick one window for each decision and write it down.

Those figures show how little data some phrases carry. They are not Keyword Planner numbers. The first comes from a different tool. The second comes from one blog's small test. Use them to set expectations, not to close a decision on their own.
Keyword Planner very low search volume: a worked example

Say you market a small app that reminds people when to water houseplants. You want to target 'soil moisture meter for monstera'. The forecast comes back blank. Do not drop the phrase yet. Run three checks in order, and write down each result before you move on.

items: Check close variants. Type the phrase with a plural, then with the words reordered. Look for any row that shows a number. A close variant may carry the average for its group.
Seed from your own page. Enter your product URL, then sort the ideas by average monthly searches. Keep any phrase that shows a number and fits what your app does.
Check Google itself. Search the phrase in your browser and read the autocomplete suggestions and related searches. If people type 'best soil moisture meter' instead, that is the phrase to test.

blocks.text: If all three checks come back empty, the phrase is probably too thin to target on its own. Keep it as a content idea if you care about it. Put paid budget into a phrase with real numbers, and recheck the blank in a month.
Find Keyword Planner and start a clean search

Open Google Ads in your browser, then go to Tools and settings > Planning > Keyword Planner. Google moves menus often. If that path has changed, search the Tools menu for Keyword Planner. Keep one browser window for the planner and another for Google Search, so you can compare results without losing your place. Press ⌘ F to find 'low search volume' on a long results page.
Mistakes that waste the most time

items: Treating a dash as zero. A dash means Google does not have enough data to calculate that number.
Changing bids to clear a Low search volume status. Google says bid, Quality Score and creative edits do not change it.
Comparing a 12-month average with a forecast from the last 7 to 10 days as if they describe the same window.
Rewriting a sensitive phrase to dodge the policy instead of choosing a neutral angle that fits the topic.
Treating a new account's forecast as final. New advertisers see averages built from all advertisers until their own data builds.
Skipping the date. Historical numbers refresh, so an undated note can mislead the whole team later.

blocks.text: Hidden data is a wider problem

Hidden data is not only a Keyword Planner issue. Ahrefs reports that anonymized queries made up 46.77% of Search Console clicks in April 2025, measured across 22 billion clicks. That is a different data source, so treat it as a warning about hidden data, not a measure of Keyword Planner gaps. The practical lesson is simple. When a number is hidden, write down what you still know and move on.

blocks.title: Client data comes first
blocks.text: If your clients work in health, finance or another regulated field, follow your employer's rules on client data. Do that before you paste an account screen into a document, a chat or Lazur. Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut, but the rules come from your employer.
Keep a log so nobody reruns the same search

Make a sheet in Google Sheets with a few columns: phrase, what the blank was, date checked, decision and owner. Share it in Slack so the team sees changes. Add a note when a row changes. The log needs no new tool. It stops the same blank from costing a new afternoon every month. For more on running a sheet like this, see [Google Sheets for marketers on Mac](/for/marketers/google-sheets). To sort the log by date, see [sort data by column in Google Sheets](/how-to/sort-data-by-column-in-google-sheets).
Where Lazur helps, and where it doesn't

Lazur explains, points, guides, drafts and dictates. It does not click buttons or operate other apps for you. You stay in charge of the account. Use Lazur for the reading, the writing and the reminders, and do the clicks yourself.

Hold ⌥ ⌘ while the results are on screen and ask what the dash means. Lazur answers out loud. Ask where the column is, and Lazur draws a circle and a label around it. Ask how to start from a website, and Lazur guides you one click at a time, waiting for each click.
What to do next

Start with the phrase that matters most to your revenue, not the one that is easiest to test. Run the three checks, write the result, and set a reminder to recheck in a month. If a phrase still shows nothing, pick a neighbor with real numbers. Or accept that the volume is unknown and test the idea as content.

blocks.title: Check the refresh timing
blocks.text: Historical volume metrics refresh monthly, according to Google's Ads API documentation. If you copied numbers into a sheet last month, they may not match the screen today. Date every copy so the team knows which numbers are current.
Some phrases stay blank for a long time. That is normal for niche terms. Keep them as ideas, date the decision, and move your attention to phrases you can measure.

faq.question: Does a blank forecast mean nobody searches for this?
faq.answer: No. Google's Low search volume status means very little to no search history on Google. A blank can also come from sensitive-category rules, unfinished account setup, or a phrase that sits inside a group of close variants. Find out which one you have before you drop the idea.

faq.question: Does a dash mean zero searches?
faq.answer: No. Google's forecast help says a dash in the impression share column means there isn't enough data to calculate that number. Treat it as unknown, not as zero.

faq.question: Will spending more money make the numbers show?
faq.answer: Google does not publish the spend level needed to see exact volumes. Some third-party blogs quote dollar amounts, but Google's pages don't back them up. Finish setup and billing first, then check the page again before you spend anything to test.

faq.question: Why did a phrase show numbers last month and a blank now?
faq.answer: Forecasts refresh daily and use the last 7 to 10 days, so they move. Historical volume metrics refresh monthly. Seasonality and changes in the data can change what you see from one month to the next.

faq.question: Should I write content for zero-volume keywords?
faq.answer: Only with a reason beyond the search number. Ahrefs' small 2022 test found zero-volume keywords averaged 11.3 impressions over 28 days, and under 1% drew more than 100. The author warns the sample was small, so treat it as a bet.

faq.question: Can Lazur fix Keyword Planner for me?
faq.answer: No. Lazur does not click buttons or operate other apps for you. It can explain what a blank means, point at the column, guide you one click at a time, draft a note for your team and set a reminder.

faq.question: Does Lazur see my Google Ads account?
faq.answer: Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer, and they are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models. Follow your employer's rules on client data before you show any account.

faq.question: Does this work on a Mac?
faq.answer: Keyword Planner runs in the Google Ads web interface, so you use a browser. The Google pages I checked do not list Mac browser requirements. If a page will not load, check Google's browser help before you change any settings.

faq.question: Why does the menu path look different for me?
faq.answer: Google Ads moves menus often. Look under Tools and settings, then Planning, then Keyword Planner. If that path is missing, search the Tools menu for Keyword Planner.

costs.title: Paid hours spent on a blank
costs.text: Marketing managers earn a median of $166,790 a year, according to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics for May 2025. Assuming a standard full-time year, that works out to about $80 an hour. That is our arithmetic, not a BLS figure, and it covers marketing managers only. If a blank column eats an afternoon, that time has a price, even if nobody logs it.

costs.title: Budget decisions made on guesses
costs.text: Keyword Planner forecasts often feed budget plans. A low or blank forecast can push you to drop a phrase that would have worked. Google says low forecasts might reflect a lack of searches for your exact phrase, so the number is not a verdict on the market. No study we found counts how often this mistake costs money. Treat it as a risk to check, not a loss you can prove.

costs.title: Hidden data pushes you toward guessing
costs.text: Ahrefs reports that anonymized queries made up 46.77% of Search Console clicks in April 2025. That is a different tool and a different data set, so it works only as an analogy. The point still holds. When data is hidden, teams guess more, and guesses take meetings and rework to correct.

costs.title: Chasing zero-volume terms
costs.text: Ahrefs ran a small test in 2022. Keywords with about 10 or fewer monthly searches averaged 11.3 Search Console impressions over 28 days, and less than 1% drew more than 100. The author calls the sample small. Writing a full page for a term like that is a bet, not a plan.

causes.title: Very little search history
causes.text: Google's Low search volume status goes to a keyword with very little to no search history on Google. New products, brand names, odd phrasing and very local terms often land here. The status describes the keyword's history, not your ad quality. Editing bids, Quality Score or creatives does not change it.

causes.title: Sensitive categories
causes.text: Google's help pages say sensitive keywords may not be discoverable or forecastable. Some health and finance terms fall in that group. Privacy and personalized advertising policies can also block those categories. You may see an error that asks you to try different keywords or URLs. The block applies to the phrase, so it says little about your idea.

causes.title: Account setup and billing not finished
causes.text: Google says you must finish account setup, including billing information, before basic features such as keyword ideas work. The help page does not give a spend level for exact numbers. Third-party blogs quote dollar figures, but those are anecdotal. Check your own account before you assume the data is missing.

causes.title: Averages and forecasts use different windows
causes.text: Average monthly searches cover a 12-month period by default. Forecasts use the last 7 to 10 days, adjusted for seasonality. A term that spiked last spring can look flat in the forecast and still strong in the average, or the reverse. Mixing the two windows makes a normal term look dead.

causes.title: New accounts borrow other advertisers' data
causes.text: New advertisers get forecasts based on historical average data for all advertisers until their own account has enough data. A low forecast can reflect the phrase itself, not your account. A dash in the impression share column means there isn't enough data to calculate it. Bid range statistics can also be missing for keywords with little bid history.

causes.title: Your phrase belongs to a bigger group
causes.text: Average monthly searches cover a keyword and its close variants. A phrase you type may show numbers that belong to a close cousin. Two spellings or word orders can also return different results. This is why one phrase can show a number while its twin shows a blank.

fixes.title: Read the message before you change anything
fixes.text: Write down exactly what you see: a dash, a blank, a Low search volume status, or an error. Each one points to a different cause. Press ⌘ F in Chrome or Safari and search for 'low search volume' to find every affected row. Do not edit bids yet.

fixes.title: Check close variants and word order
fixes.text: Type the phrase, then its plural, then the word order a customer would use. Add a city only if local searches matter to your business. Keep notes on which versions return numbers. Close variants share a combined average, so a version with a number may stand in for the one you want.

fixes.title: Seed from a website instead of a phrase
fixes.text: When the error asks you to try different keywords or URLs, try a URL. Enter your own product page or a competitor's category page as the starting point. Then sort the ideas by average monthly searches. You learn which phrases real pages already use. This only needs your Google Ads login.

fixes.title: Search Google and read the results page
fixes.text: Type the phrase into Google Search in your browser. Read the autocomplete suggestions, the related searches at the bottom, and any People also ask boxes. No volume number appears there. You do learn the words people actually type, and that often gives you a usable neighbor phrase.

fixes.title: Check your own Search Console queries
fixes.text: If your site already gets traffic, open the Performance report in Google Search Console and read the queries. Some queries are hidden as anonymized. Ahrefs found that share was large in April 2025, so don't expect a full list. Use what shows and mark the rest as unknown.

fixes.title: Finish account setup and billing
fixes.text: Open Google Ads and finish any setup prompts, including billing. Google says basic features such as keyword ideas need it. Google does not publish a spend level for exact volumes, so don't spend money just to see them. Ask whoever owns the account for its billing status.

fixes.title: Check the status before you touch bids
fixes.text: If a keyword in your campaign shows Low search volume, leave the bid alone. Google's definition says bid, Quality Score and creative edits do not change the status. Google re-checks it regularly, and its page says about a week. Decide to keep, pause or swap the keyword, and write the date next to your choice.

fixes.title: Match the forecast window to the average
fixes.text: Compare the 12-month average with the recent forecast before you decide. For seasonal products, read the trend in the chart, not one number. For a new brand, expect blanks for a while and recheck monthly. Google's Ads API documentation says historical volume metrics refresh monthly.

fixes.title: Set a fallback with real volume
fixes.text: If the phrase stays blank, pick a nearby term that does show numbers and build the main plan on it. Keep the blank phrase for brand or content work only if you still believe in it. A fallback you can measure beats a guess you cannot check.

fixes.title: Log the decision with a date
fixes.text: Put the phrase, what Keyword Planner showed, the date and your decision in one row of a shared sheet. Recheck in a month. Dated notes stop the team from rerunning the same search every week. Follow your employer's rules on client data before you add any client name.

plan.label: Morning
plan.title: Read the blank before you touch bids
plan.text: Open the Keyword Planner results in your browser. Write down which blank you see for each phrase: a dash, a low volume status, or an error. Do not change bids yet. This takes a few minutes and keeps you from fixing the wrong problem.

plan.label: Late morning
plan.title: Test variants and a website seed
plan.text: Type each phrase with its plural and its word-order variant. Then start a search from your product URL and sort the ideas by average monthly searches. Note which versions return numbers in your shared sheet.

plan.label: Afternoon
plan.title: Check Google and your own queries
plan.text: Search each phrase in Google and read the autocomplete suggestions and related searches. In Search Console, open the Performance report and read the queries that already bring clicks. Record one line of learning for each phrase.

plan.label: Afternoon
plan.title: Confirm account setup and billing
plan.text: Ask the account owner whether setup and billing are finished. If Google Ads shows an open setup prompt, finish it. If the business sits in a sensitive category, plan neutral phrasing before you write anything.

plan.label: Next week
plan.title: Recheck the status and decide
plan.text: Recheck the status and the forecast. If a keyword still shows Low search volume, decide to keep, pause or swap it. Set a reminder in Apple Reminders so the recheck actually happens.

plan.label: Monthly
plan.title: Refresh the log with dates
plan.text: Historical volume metrics refresh monthly. Update the numbers and the dates in your sheet, and mark rows that changed. Keep the history, so the team can see why a phrase was dropped.
